newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's 1998 budget paves way for EMU membership.
newsitem.headline: Spain's 1998 budget paves way for EMU membership.

text.p: Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato unveiled on Friday the framework of a 1998 budget package that economists say is realistic and will underpin Spain's drive to take part in the launch of Europe's common currency.

Spain's conservative government has pledged to bring the budget deficit down to 2.4 percent of gross domestic product from a projected three percent this year, partly through an accelerating economic growth rate, which is seen rising to 3.4 percent in 1998 from 3.2 percent in 1997.
"We are looking at a clear, sustainable recovery and this budget is going to be a key factor in the recovery," Rato told a news conference. "It is going to set the basis for the recovery."

The budget draft, which must be presented to the legislature by the end of September, aims for growth and fiscal austerity and sends a signal to Spain's wary neighbours that it has renounced lax finances and converted to a model of fiscal sobriety.
"I have to admit, grudgingly, that they have done a good job. They (the numbers) look realistic," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

If anything, economists say, most of the government's numbers do more than just add up. After years of scorn from international financial circles, Spain's public finances now look good -- and even better than it is admitting.
"Growth of 3.4 percent might even be too modest. I'd put in higher," Lumholdt said.
One growth driver is expected to be private consumption, which is seen rising by 3.0 percent this year and 3.1 percent in 1997, the government said.
A pick-up in public sector consumption, following a decline in 1997, and strong rises in construction and capital goods will also add to the recovery.

"I think the numbers are realistic. They will add up because of economic growth and because of the reduction of the interest burden after lower official rates," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
"This is a budget of continuation and could have been even more aggressive. It is a step toward the convergence plan and bringing the deficit to 1.6 percent of GDP in 2000," she said.

With this budget, the conservative government's second since it ousted the Socialists last Spring after 13 years in power, Spain seems set to meet all of the Economic and Monetary Union economic criteria by a healthy margin.

While economists argued Spain may be unable to bring its budget deficit down to 2.4 percent of GDP as promised, it should manage to keep it below the key 3.0 percent level which forms one of the key Maastricht requirements.

Although it is the 1997 budget and its numbers that are tested for fitness to participate in the single currency launch, the 1998 budget proves that this year's efforts were not a one-off and that Spain is committed to keeping its fiscal house in order.
"This budget continues on the good path. It is sustainable and with it we will enter European economic and monetary union," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
